full_text_sections.results: 3Results3.1Overall pathogen distribution and demographicsAcross 36 surveillance months we identified 2,597 virologically confirmed pediatric LRTI cases. HRV was the most frequently detected virus (796 cases, 30.7%), followed by ADV (692, 26.6%), RSV (536, 20.6%), HBoV (313, 12.1%), IFV (155, 6.0%) and HMPV (105, 4.0%) (Figure 2A; Table 1). Sputum was the predominant specimen type for HRV, RSV, HBoV, HMPV and IFV. The proportion of cases sampled from the lower airway (sputum or BALF) likewise differed across pathogens (χ2 = 73.7, df = 5, p < 0.001), ranging from 70.1% for ADV and 70.5% for HMPV to 88.5% for HBoV (Table 1). ADV was more evenly distributed across specimen types, with BALF (35.4%) and sputum (34.7%) contributing similar shares and nasopharyngeal swabs a further 29.6%, giving ADV a markedly higher BALF share than the other five viruses (Figure 2B). Annual case counts rose from 188 in 2023 to 1,027 in 2024 and 1,382 in 2025 (Figure 2C). The 2023 figures warrant particular caution on this account. The assay reached full clinical implementation only in the fourth quarter of that year (Section 2.2), so the 188 cases recorded in 2023 almost certainly under-represent circulation during the early post-pandemic period relative to 2024 and 2025, when testing volume was broadly stable. Subsequent analyses therefore emphasize pathogen composition, age distribution and seasonal timing, which are far less sensitive to testing volume than absolute case counts.Figure 2Overall pathogen spectrum and specimen characteristics of pediatric viral LRTI in Tianjin, 2023–2025. (A) Case distribution across the six viral pathogens, ranked by prevalence. (B) Specimen-type composition by pathogen. (C) Annual case burden, stacked by pathogen.Grouped bar and stacked bar chart panel showing (A) case numbers and percentages for six pathogens, (B) specimen composition by pathogen, and (C) annual case burden from 2023 to 2025. HRV and ADV have the highest positive cases, sputum is the most common specimen, and total case burden increases each year, with pathogen contribution shown by color.Two features of the assay bound the influence of testing volume without removing it. All six viruses sit on a single multiplex panel and are screened simultaneously in every specimen, so no virus could be tested more often than another, and a change in ordering volume alters which children were tested rather than which viruses were sought. What this cannot exclude is a shift in case mix: if tNGS was ordered preferentially for more severely ill children, and if the pathogen spectrum of severe admissions differs from that of milder ones, composition will move with ordering practice. The markedly higher BALF share of ADV (Figure 2B) is consistent with such a gradient, and the point is developed in Section 4.6.Boys predominated for HRV (59.2%, p<0.001), ADV (61.4%, p<0.001), RSV (56.7%, p=0.002), HBoV (57.2%, p=0.013) and HMPV (62.9%, p=0.011), whereas IFV showed a balanced sex ratio (53.5% male, p=0.42) (Table 1; Figure 3A). Although IFV was the only virus without a male excess, a χ2 test for heterogeneity across the six pathogens did not reach significance (χ2 = 5.77, df = 5, p = 0.33), and neither did the comparison of IFV against the other five viruses combined (χ2 = 1.68, df = 1, p = 0.20). The balanced ratio for IFV is therefore better read as a failure to demonstrate a male excess in the smallest of the larger groups (n = 155) than as evidence of a genuinely different sex distribution.Figure 3Demographic composition of pediatric viral LRTI by pathogen. (A) Sex distribution, with binomial-test significance markers. (B) Age (years) by pathogen (median, IQR), with jittered individual data points overlaid. Significance markers: *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001; ns = not significant.Bar chart on the left shows male and female sex distribution for six pathogens with males consistently higher for HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV, and HMPV; differences denoted by statistical significance symbols. Boxplot on the right displays age distribution in years for each pathogen with medians, interquartile ranges, and data points, indicating variation in median ages by pathogen.Age distributions differed sharply across pathogens (Kruskal–Wallis H = 372.7, p < 0.001; Figure 3B). Infants and toddlers carried most HBoV (median 2.0 [IQR 1.0–4.0] years) and RSV (3.0 [1.0–4.0]) cases; preschoolers were the main group for HRV (4.0 [2.0–6.0]) and HMPV (4.0 [1.8–6.0]); ADV predominated in school-aged children (6.0 [3.0–8.0]), while IFV spanned the older preschool-to-school-age range (median 5.0 [2.0–7.0]) (Table 1; Figure 3B).3.2Temporal distributionMonthly time-series of the six pathogens (Figure 4A) showed strong but pathogen-specific seasonality. HRV, ADV, RSV, IFV and HMPV all reached their annual maxima in December, consistent with the cold, dry continental winter being the dominant transmission season in northern China. The December peak of late 2024 (about 400 positive cases that month) was the largest monthly count of the surveillance period, with a smaller but still notable winter peak in December 2025. HBoV behaved differently, showing a single summer maximum in July. ADV showed a secondary peak in late spring (April–May), and HRV and ADV together produced the broadest seasonal envelope (March–December) of any pathogen. The seasonal heatmap (Figure 4B) summarizes these patterns: each virus shows at least one clearly defined month-of-year peak, and HBoV is the only virus to peak in a warm-season month (July). Because the heatmap is normalized row-wise, color intensity for each pathogen is scaled to its own monthly range; the visual prominence of a peak for a low-incidence pathogen (for example, HMPV) therefore does not indicate the same absolute case count as for a high-incidence pathogen (for example, HRV).Figure 4Temporal distribution of pediatric viral LRTI, 2023–2025. (A) Stacked monthly case counts by pathogen. (B) Seasonal heatmap of mean monthly cases by pathogen; cell shading is normalized row-wise so that each pathogen’s twelve-month profile can be read on a comparable scale.Stacked bar chart and heatmap visualizing monthly viral pathogen detections from January 2023 to December 2025. The chart (panel A) shows case counts for HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV, IFV, and HMPV, with peaks observed between late 2024 and early 2025. The heatmap (panel B) presents mean cases per month for each virus, highlighting increased relative intensity for most pathogens in November and December, with values labeled within cells and a scale indicating intensity from low (yellow) to high (red).3.3Seasonal and meteorological analyses3.3.1Overall pathogen–climate correlationsOverall Spearman rank correlations (Figure 5A; Table 2) showed a significant positive correlation between HBoV and temperature (ρ = +0.34, p = 0.04). ADV (ρ = +0.32, p = 0.06), HRV (ρ = +0.28, p = 0.10) and RSV (ρ = +0.24, p = 0.16) showed positive but non-significant trends. full_text_sections.discussion: 4DiscussionIn this three-year, single-center cohort we characterized the post-pandemic epidemiology of pediatric viral LRTI in Tianjin, a megacity on the North China Plain, and quantified how closely monthly viral activity tracks ambient weather. To our knowledge, the dataset is unusual for northern China in spanning six respiratory viruses, including the comparatively under-surveyed HRV, HBoV and HMPV, over the full 2023–2025 post-pandemic rebound window, with a complete and time-matched monthly meteorological record.4.1Principal epidemiological featuresAcross the six viruses, HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading causes of pediatric LRTI, and each pathogen carried a well-defined demographic profile. Age and sex stratification confirmed recognized biological gradients. RSV and HBoV were most prevalent in infants and toddlers, in line with airway and immune development (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022); ADV peaked in school-aged children and IFV in the older preschool-to-school-age range, consistent with close-contact transmission in schools and other crowded settings (Fang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023); and HMPV showed an intermediate distribution. The older age skew of IFV fits its epidemiology in temperate regions, where school-aged children are the principal drivers of seasonal influenza transmission and the group in which symptomatic infection is most readily recognized, in contrast to the infant and toddler predominance of RSV and HBoV (Feng et al., 2024; Klein and Flanagan, 2016). The male predominance for HRV, ADV, RSV, HBoV and HMPV, but not IFV, echoes prior pediatric LRTI cohorts and may reflect sex differences in innate immunity and behavior (Klein and Flanagan, 2016). The strong age-group × pathogen association reinforces the need for an explicitly age-stratified surveillance framework.The six pathogens also fell into two distinct seasonal groups. HRV, ADV, RSV, IFV and HMPV all peaked in December, during the cold, dry continental winter, whereas HBoV stood apart with an isolated July maximum—the only warm-season peak of the panel. HRV additionally displayed the broadest seasonal envelope, circulating from March to December, consistent with fundamentally endemic, weakly seasonal behavior. Because the rise in absolute case counts partly reflects expanding testing volume rather than incidence (Section 3.1), the interpretation that follows rests on pathogen composition, age structure and seasonal timing rather than on raw counts.4.2Interpretation in the post-pandemic contextThese patterns are best read against, rather than directly measured against, pre-pandemic Chinese pediatric surveillance, since our cohort describes the post-pandemic period without a matched pre-pandemic Tianjin comparator. Several multi-center Chinese studies contrasting pre-pandemic (2018–2019) with post-pandemic (2023 onward) cohorts have reported a broadly consistent post-pandemic pattern: higher overall pathogen positivity and mixed-infection rates, a higher proportion of severe presentations, and shifts in the relative ranking, seasonal timing and age distribution of individual pathogens (Cui et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). In Shanghai, post-pandemic test positivity rose markedly relative to 2019, with both RSV and ADV increasing and RSV’s onset shifting earlier into August, ahead of its conventional winter season (Liu et al., 2025); other Chinese cohorts spanning the pre-pandemic, pandemic and post-pandemic phases have likewise documented altered seasonal timing and age-distribution shifts for RSV, ADV and rhinovirus after non-pharmaceutical interventions were relaxed (Cui et al., 2024).Interpreted against this backdrop, our Tianjin observations show both continuities and departures. HRV’s endemic, weakly seasonal circulation—reflected in its leading position and broad March–December envelope—appears to have been less perturbed by the pandemic and its aftermath than that of the more strongly seasonal viruses. By contrast, the convergence of five of the six viruses onto a single sharp December peak is consistent with the compressed, intensified post-pandemic winter surge described elsewhere in China, plausibly reflecting the accumulated immunity debt from population-level exposure gaps in 2020–2022 (Cohen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024) superimposed on the resumption of normal contact patterns. HBoV departed most sharply from this winter pattern, peaking instead in summer; to our knowledge, such an isolated warm-season peak has not been prominently reported as a post-pandemic phenomenon elsewhere in China. Whether it reflects a genuine post-pandemic shift in HBoV’s seasonal niche or a feature specific to Tianjin’s continental climate cannot be resolved with a single-center, single-period dataset, and we return to its biological and clinical significance in Section 4.4.4.3Climate-driven lagged effectsThe unadjusted and seasonally adjusted analyses answer different questions, and reading them together guards against a common pitfall in climate–infection studies. In the unadjusted analysis (Table 3), IFV appeared the most climate-responsive virus, with antecedent humidity and temperature aligning with later case counts, in keeping with the recognized seasonal phasing of influenza in temperate climates (Deyle et al., 2016; Kudo et al., 2019; Lowen et al., 2007; Lowen and Steel, 2014). Once seasonality and secular trend were held constant in the unified model, however, these IFV associations disappeared (Table 5). This does not mean that IFV has no climatic drivers. Rather, because ambient temperature and humidity in Tianjin themselves follow an almost perfect annual sinusoid, they are nearly collinear with the sine–cosine seasonal terms of the unified model; for a virus as tightly locked to the annual cycle as influenza (77.5% of deviance explained by season and trend alone), the model simply cannot separate the effect of “season” from that of “temperature” or “humidity.” The most that can be concluded is that, at the present monthly resolution, IFV shows no climatic association detectable independently of the seasonal cycle itself.The seasonally adjusted model instead isolated RSV and HMPV as the only viruses with climate associations independent of shared seasonality (Table 5): RSV tracked temperature and wind speed at short lags, while HMPV tracked temperature positively and humidity inversely, although its low case counts make these estimates imprecise and hypothesis-generating. HRV, ADV and HBoV showed no independent lagged signal, indicating that at monthly resolution their seasonal envelopes are not accompanied by a detectable climate effect beyond the annual cycle. This null result should not be read as evidence of climatic insensitivity. For these three viruses the seasonal-plus-trend baseline itself explained comparatively little of the monthly deviance (HRV 41.5%, HBoV 28.6%, ADV 17.1%; Table 4), so a large share of the variation in their case counts is left unaccounted for by season, trend and weather combined. Residual variation of that magnitude widens the standard errors, and with 36 monthly observations spanning three seasonal cycles only associations of substantial size could reach significance. A modest but real climate effect would probably have escaped detection here, and the finding is better described as uninformative for HRV, ADV and HBoV than as negative. The contrast between the two analyses carries the key methodological lesson: lagged climate associations in surveillance data can be interpreted only after seasonality has been accounted for.These post-pandemic patterns can be read against the pre-pandemic national baseline of Xu et al. (2021), who modelled a seven-virus panel—five of them shared with our own—across 81 sentinel hospitals in 22 Chinese provinces (2009–2013) and ranked the meteorological factors by climate region. For the temperate north, to which Tianjin belongs, three points agree wit…
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5ConclusionAcross 36 months of post-pandemic surveillance in Tianjin (2,597 confirmed cases), HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading viral causes of pediatric LRTI, and each of the six viruses carried a distinctive age, sex, seasonal and specimen-type profile. In a unified model adjusting simultaneously for seasonality and secular trend, RSV and HMPV, rather than IFV, showed the clearest evidence of an independent, non-seasonal climate association, whereas IFV’s prominent unadjusted climate signal proved to reflect its strong intrinsic seasonality. HBoV showed a singular July epidemic at odds with the December convergence of the other viruses, together providing a preliminary basis for pathogen-tailored early warning and prevention in northern Chinese megacities. Co-infection occurred in 4.5% of positives, centered on HRV-containing combinations whose clinical severity remains to be defined. Set alongside pre-pandemic Chinese pediatric surveillance, these findings are broadly consistent with a post-pandemic pattern of intensified, temporally compressed winter transmission, while HBoV’s summer epidemic appears to be a locally distinctive feature warranting further study. If confirmed with higher-resolution, denominator-based data, these findings could inform a hospital-level operational calendar anchored on the December peak and the secondary July HBoV peak, climate-informed early warning tailored to each pathogen’s actual (seasonally adjusted) climate sensitivity, and a refined strategy for vaccination, RSV passive immunization and infection control. Such confirmation will require multi-center cohorts, denominator-based positivity metrics, weekly- or daily-resolution meteorology, and direct pre- versus post-pandemic comparison.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionLower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs)—comprising pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and related lower-airway syndromes—remain leading causes of pediatric hospitalization and mortality in children under five worldwide, with viruses accounting for the overwhelming majority of cases (Nair et al., 2010; Mulholland, 2003; Li et al., 2022). In contrast to generally self-limiting upper respiratory infections, viral LRTIs account disproportionately for admissions requiring supplemental oxygen and intensive care; moreover, certain pathogens, notably RSV and HRV, are implicated in long-term sequelae including recurrent wheeze and asthma (Li et al., 2022; Bizot et al., 2021; Royston and Tapparel, 2016). In China, the burden is amplified by dense urban populations, overlapping pathogen circulation, and the high contact rates among school-aged children, all of which sustain substantial LRTI-related hospitalizations (Cui et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Following the lifting of pandemic-era non-pharmaceutical interventions, several Chinese regions reported atypical, out-of-season resurgences of RSV, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, and ADV (Del Riccio et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). These have been attributed both to an immunity gap accumulated during 2020–2022 and to the re-establishment of pre-pandemic transmission networks (Cohen et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024). Despite this evolving landscape, most national surveillance efforts remain narrowly focused on classical pathogens (RSV, ADV, IFV) or aggregate all respiratory infections irrespective of anatomical site. Consequently, the post-pandemic, multi-pathogen epidemiology of viral LRTI specifically in children—particularly at the city level, where targeted surveillance is most actionable—remains inadequately characterized (Terliesner et al., 2022; Xia et al., 2026).Ambient weather conditions are well-established modulators of respiratory virus transmission, operating through both physical and host-defense mechanisms (Baker et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021). Cold, dry air favors the persistence and airborne dispersal of enveloped viruses such as RSV and influenza by stabilizing the lipid envelope, slowing droplet evaporation, and impairing upper-airway mucociliary clearance (Kudo et al., 2019; Lowen et al., 2007; Lowen and Steel, 2014). Non-enveloped viruses, including ADV and HBoV, whose protein capsids tolerate a wider range of environmental stressors, tend to circulate more evenly throughout the year (Chen et al., 2014b; Lion, 2014). Importantly, climate–virus relationships are non-linear and time-delayed; exposures occurring days to weeks before case surges often exert the dominant effect, a structure that makes distributed lag non-linear models (DLNMs) particularly suitable for fine-grained inference (Bhaskaran et al., 2013; Gasparrini et al., 2010; Gasparrini, 2011). A recent post-pandemic study from Wuhan, in central China, applied daily-resolution DLNMs to seven respiratory pathogens and identified distinct lagged climate patterns—most notably, humidity drops as 1–2-week antecedents of RSV surges and wind speed as a leading correlate of influenza activity (Li et al., 2025). Because only monthly-resolution meteorological data were available for the present 2023–2025 window (Section 2.3), a full DLNM cross-basis was not identifiable with the available degrees of freedom; we therefore adapted the same distributed-lag logic into a screening framework of single-lag quasi-Poisson models spanning 0–6-month lags, cross-validated against cross-correlation functions and, in a second step, adjusted for seasonality and secular trend within a unified model (Section 2.4). This approach is best viewed as a monthly-resolution approximation to the DLNM framework rather than a full non-linear cross-basis estimation.However, few studies have systematically examined this multi-pathogen landscape in northern China, where the continental monsoon climate—characterized by cold, dry winters; hot, humid summers; and pronounced seasonal swings in temperature, humidity, and wind—differs markedly from the subtropical conditions of Wuhan and other southern cities (Chen et al., 2014a; Cui et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2023). Tianjin, a megacity of 13 million on the North China Plain, offers a particularly valuable setting to address this gap. Its local viral spectrum extends beyond the four classical agents to include three pathogens that are less consistently surveilled but contribute substantially to pediatric LRTI: HRV, HBoV, and HMPV (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2020). Prior work in this area has concentrated largely on southern China or on the classical pathogens (RSV, ADV, IFV), and the lagged climatic effects of the less consistently surveilled HRV, HBoV and HMPV under a temperate continental climate have not been systematically evaluated. Precisely how these three viruses, alongside the classical agents, track climatic exposures across different lag intervals in northern China therefore remains poorly characterized—a knowledge gap that has direct implications for the design of climate-informed early-warning systems in the region.To address this, we analyzed three years of post-pandemic surveillance data (January 2023 to December 2025) from a tertiary children’s hospital in Tianjin, encompassing 2,597 virologically confirmed pediatric LRTI cases caused by six respiratory viruses. Our objectives were: (i) to describe the demographic, temporal, and specimen-type distributions of each pathogen; (ii) to characterize co-infection patterns; (iii) to test pathogen-specific associations with monthly meteorological variables using Spearman correlation and season-stratified analyses; and (iv) to evaluate lagged climate effects across 0- to 6-month intervals using cross-correlation functions and a unified quasi-Poisson generalized linear model that simultaneously adjusts for seasonality and secular trends. Finally, we discuss the practical implications of our findings for climate-informed early-warning systems and pathogen-tailored preventive strategies in northern Chinese megacities. 2.2Pathogen detectionRespiratory specimens (sputum, the predominant type; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, BALF; nasopharyngeal swabs; and oropharyngeal swabs) were collected following standardized clinical protocols, placed into viral transport medium, and transported within two hours at 2–8 °C to the clinical laboratory. Total nucleic acids were extracted on an automated platform following the manufacturer’s instructions. All specimens were tested with the same commercial targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) panel, which simultaneously screens for respiratory bacteria, viruses, atypical pathogens and antimicrobial-resistance markers. Library construction, ultra-multiplex amplification of pathogen-specific genomic regions and Illumina-compatible high-throughput sequencing were performed following the manufacturer’s recommended workflow, with reads aligned against a curated pathogen reference database (Li et al., 2025; Shang et al., 2025). The vendor’s reporting algorithm assigned each detected organism a clinical pathogenicity grade, from Class A (highest confidence) through lower-confidence grades. The panel was introduced during 2023 and reached full clinical implementation in the fourth quarter of that year, after which testing volume remained broadly stable through 2024 and 2025. Monthly counts of tNGS requests could not be retrieved from the laboratory information system for the whole study window, so this account of testing volume rests on the laboratory’s implementation record rather than on an auditable series of test counts, and it should be read as such.The grade is a composite call rather than a single read-count cut-off. It is generated by an integrated scoring system that combines normalized read counts (reads per million, RPM), the breadth of genome coverage achieved across the targeted regions, and spec…

elements_en.research_question_and_background: (C) Annual case burden, stacked by pathogen.Grouped bar and stacked bar chart panel showing (A) case numbers and percentages for six pathogens, (B) specimen composition by pathogen, and (C) annual case burden from 2023 to 2025.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: HRV was the most frequently detected virus (796 cases, 30.7%), followed by ADV (692, 26.6%), RSV (536, 20.6%), HBoV (313, 12.1%), IFV (155, 6.0%) and HMPV (105, 4.0%) (Figure 2A; Table 1).
elements_en.methods: Pathogen–climate associations were estimated using a quasi-Poisson model that adjusted for seasonality, secular trend, and lagged meteorological exposures.ResultsAmong 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%), and HMPV (4.0%).
elements_en.main_results: RSV and HBoV were most prevalent in infants and toddlers, in line with airway and immune development (Feng et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2022); ADV peaked in school-aged children and IFV in the older preschool-to-school-age range, consistent with close-contact transmission in schools and other crowded settings (Fang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023); and HMPV showed an intermediate distribution.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: To our knowledge, the dataset is unusual for northern China in spanning six respiratory viruses, including the comparatively under-surveyed HRV, HBoV and HMPV, over the full 2023–2025 post-pandemic rebound window, with a complete and time-matched monthly meteorological record.4.1Principal epidemiological featuresAcross the six viruses, HRV, ADV and RSV were the leading causes of pediatric LRTI, and each pathogen carried a well-defined demographic profile.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The strong age-group × pathogen association reinforces the need for an explicitly age-stratified surveillance framework.The six pathogens also fell into two distinct seasonal groups.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Co-infection occurred in 4.5% of positives, centered on HRV-containing combinations whose clinical severity remains to be defined.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: (C) 按病原体分组的年度病例负担。分组条形图和堆叠条形图面板显示(A)六种病原体的病例数和百分比,(B)标本组成按病原体分组,以及(C)2023至2025年的年度病例负担。
elements_zh.methods: 使用准泊松模型估计病原体与气候的关联,该模型考虑了季节性、长期趋势和滞后气象暴露因素。结果:在2,597例病毒阳性病例中,主要病原体为HRV(30.7%)、ADV(26.6%)和RSV(20.6%),随后是HBoV(12.1%)、IFV(6.0%)和HMPV(4.0%)。
elements_zh.main_results: RSV和HBoV在婴儿和幼儿中最为常见,这与气道和免疫系统发育一致(Feng等,2024;Jiang等,2016;Li等,2022);ADV在学龄儿童中达到高峰,IFV在较大的学龄前至学龄儿童群体中达到高峰,这与学校及其他拥挤环境中的密切接触有关(Fang等,2025;Yu等,2021;Zhang等,2023);而HMPV则表现出中间分布。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 据我们所知,该数据集在北方中国较为罕见,因为它涵盖了2023–2025年疫情后反弹期间的六种呼吸道病毒,包括相对较少被调查的HRV、HBoV和HMPV,并且具有完整且时间匹配的每月气象记录。4.1主要流行病学特征:在六种病毒中,HRV、ADV和RSV是导致儿童下呼吸道感染的主要原因,每种病原体都有明确的流行病学特征。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 强年龄组 × 病原体关联进一步强调了需要一个明确的年龄分层监测框架。这六种病原体也分为两个不同的季节性群体。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 在阳性病例中有4.5%发生了共感染,主要集中在包含HRV的组合中,其临床严重程度仍需进一步定义。

title_zh: 中国天津市2023–2025年儿童下呼吸道感染的流行病学及滞后气候驱动因素
source_body_en: BackgroundFollowing the lifting of pandemic-era restrictions, China experienced a sharp resurgence in pediatric respiratory infections; however, post-pandemic epidemiological and climatic data on lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) from the temperate continental climate of northern China remain scarce.MethodsIn this retrospective, single-center surveillance study, we characterized the post-pandemic epidemiology of six respiratory viruses in children hospitalized with LRTI in Tianjin and assessed their pathogen-specific, lagged climatic associations. 2Materials and methods2.1Study design, setting and populationWe conducted a retrospective single-center surveillance study at the Department of Respiratory Medicine, Tianjin Children’s Hospital (Ma-Chang campus), the only tertiary-A comprehensive children’s hospital in Tianjin. This last criterion operated at the level of the child rather than of the laboratory result: whenever the tNGS report carried a Class A detection of a bacterial, atypical or non-panel viral pathogen alongside one of the six target viruses, the case was removed from the cohort at eligibility screening, so no such child contributes to any analysis reported here. Children aged 0–18 years hospitalized between January 2023 and December 2025 were tested by targeted next-generation sequencing for human rhinovirus (HRV), adenovirus (ADV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human bocavirus (HBoV), influenza virus (IFV), and human metapneumovirus (HMPV). Pathogen–climate associations were estimated using a quasi-Poisson model that adjusted for seasonality, secular trend, and lagged meteorological exposures.ResultsAmong 2,597 virus-positive cases, the leading pathogens were HRV (30.7%), ADV (26.6%), and RSV (20.6%), followed by HBoV (12.1%), IFV (6.0%),...
abstract_zh: 背景:在解除疫情管控措施后,中国经历了儿童呼吸道感染的急剧回升;然而,关于来自中国北方大陆性气候地区的下呼吸道感染(LRTIs)的疫情后流行病学和气候数据仍然稀缺。方法:本研究是一项回顾性单中心监测研究,我们描述了2023–2025年疫情后天津市住院儿童中六种呼吸道病毒的流行病学,并评估了这些病毒的病原体特异性及滞后气候关联。2材料与方法2.1研究设计、设置和人群:我们在天津市儿童医院(马场校区)呼吸科开展了一项回顾性单中心监测研究,这是天津市唯一的三级甲等综合性儿童医院。这一标准适用于儿童而非实验室结果:每当tNGS报告中检测到细菌、非典型或非检测面板病毒病原体的同时也检测到六种目标病毒之一时,该病例将在资格筛选时被排除,因此没有这样的儿童参与本研究中报告的任何分析。2023年1月至2025年12月期间住院的0–18岁儿童接受了针对人类鼻病毒(HRV)、腺病毒(ADV)、呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)、人类博卡病毒(HBoV)、流感病毒(IFV)和人偏肺病毒(HMPV)的靶向下一代测序检测。使用准泊松模型估计病原体与气候的关联,该模型考虑了季节性、长期趋势和滞后气象暴露。结果:在2,597例病毒阳性病例中,主要病原体为HRV(30.7%)、ADV(26.6%)和RSV(20.6%),随后是HBoV(12.1%)、IFV(6.0%)和HMPV(4.0%)(图2A;表1)
